title: Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0)
subtitle: HTTP, extended to brew coffee, and the origin of “418 I’m a teapot”
summary: HTCPCP is a joke protocol, published on 1 April 1998, that extends HTTP with the methods, header fields and status codes needed to control a networked coffee pot. It adds a BREW method, a WHEN method for saying when enough milk has been poured, an Accept-Additions header for milk and syrup, and the famous 418 I'm a teapot response. It is written with a straight face and is a parody of how real protocol documents are written.

eli5.summary: This is a pretend rulebook for talking to a coffee machine over the internet, written as a joke. If you ask a teapot to make coffee, it politely says it can’t, because it’s a teapot.

questions: what does error 418 i'm a teapot mean
what is the brew method in http
what is the coffee uri scheme

tldr.problem: In 1998 everything was heading onto the web, and the author asked what a control protocol for a networked coffee pot would look like if written in earnest.
tldr.mechanism: It reuses HTTP, adding the BREW and WHEN methods (and borrowing PROPFIND from WebDAV), an Accept-Additions header, a Safe header extension, a coffee: URI scheme, and the status codes 406 and 418.
tldr.outcome: Nobody is meant to deploy it, but its 418 status code became a beloved Internet in-joke that still appears in web frameworks and HTTP registries.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2324 was published on 1 April 1998 as an Informational memo by Larry Masinter, then at Xerox PARC. Its abstract says HTCPCP is “a protocol for controlling, monitoring, and diagnosing coffee pots.” The memo is a parody: it imitates the dry, formal tone of a real specification while making a deliberately silly argument.

Its rationale section argues that networked appliances are coming, cites the CMU Coke machine and the Internet Toaster (a device controlled over SNMP, shown in 1990) as precedents, and concludes that “there is a strong, dark, rich requirement” for a coffee protocol. It then bases the design on HTTP 1.1 (RFC 2068) with a circular argument that ends “it is good to base HTCPCP on HTTP.”

The status text is explicit: the memo “does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.” It is Informational and was an April 1st joke, but its technical shape is a faithful HTTP extension.
sections.eli5: Imagine writing very serious grown-up rules for how to talk to a coffee machine, with lots of proper words, as a joke. That’s this document. It pretends coffee machines are going to be on the internet and need rules, and it makes the rules by borrowing the ones that web pages already use.

sections.title: Design: HTTP with Coffee Added
sections.content:
HTCPCP is “built on top of HTTP, with the addition of a few new methods, header fields and return codes.” Servers are addressed with a new coffee: URI scheme. Everything else, such as request lines, headers, status codes and bodies, is ordinary HTTP.

The memo also recommends using port 80, so that the protocol “will get all of HTTP’s firewall-crossing virtues.” It jokes that coffee pots use no fire, so firewalls are unnecessary, and then that home firewalls should protect against heat.

Reuse, don’t reinvent
Existing HTTP machinery carries the commands; HTCPCP only adds vocabulary.
Physical resources
The resources behind a coffee URI are physical objects, and the memo notes that “the data for most coffee URIs contain no caffeine.”
sections.eli5: Rather than invent a brand new language, the coffee machine just speaks the same language as websites, with a few extra words for coffee things.

sections.title: New and Reused Methods
sections.content:
Commands go to a pot with BREW or POST, carrying a message body. A pot “MUST accept both the BREW and POST method equivalently,” although using POST to cause actions is deprecated. The stated reason is that “POST may be a trademark for coffee.”

GET keeps its HTTP meaning, but the memo points out that coffee resources are physical, not information. PROPFIND, from WebDAV, is used to find metadata about the brewed resource. WHEN is for the moment milk is being poured: “Enough? Say WHEN.”

The memo contradicts itself on the body type. Section 2.1.1 says the body has Content-Type application/coffee-pot-command, while Section 4 says it MUST be message/coffeepot. Section 4 defines the body as just start or stop.
sections.eli5: You tell the machine what to do with a word like BREW. There is also a word, WHEN, for saying “stop pouring the milk, that’s enough!”

sections.title: Header Fields and Return Codes
sections.content:
HTCPCP recommends one existing header and defines one new one. It extends the Safe response header from a separate draft so that the value can be yes, no, or a condition written if- plus a token, such as if-user-awake, because whether brewing again is safe depends on who is awake.

The new Accept-Additions request header lists things the client would like added: milk types (Cream, Half-and-half, Whole-milk, Part-Skim, Skim, Non-Dairy), syrups (Vanilla, Almond, Raspberry, Chocolate), and alcohol (Whisky, Rum, Kahlua, Aquavit). The grammar also mentions sweetener and spice types but never defines them. Decaffeinated coffee is dismissed: “What’s the point?”

Two status codes get special treatment. 406 Not Acceptable may be returned if the pot cannot supply a requested addition, with a list of available additions in the body. 418 I’m a teapot is the answer to “any attempt to brew coffee with a teapot,” and the body “MAY be short and stout.”
sections.eli5: You can ask for extras like milk or syrup. If the machine can’t do it, it says “not acceptable.” If you ask a teapot for coffee, it says “I’m a teapot”, because it cannot make coffee, however nicely you ask.

sections.title: The coffee: URI Scheme
sections.content:
Coffee pots are named with a URI scheme that can be spelled with the word for coffee in any of 29 languages, percent-encoded as UTF-8. The ABNF is coffee-url = coffee-scheme ":" [ "//" host ] ["/" pot-designator ] ["?" additions-list ], and a pot designator looks like pot- followed by an integer, for machines with several pots.

The scheme list includes koffie, coffee, kaffe, kahvi, and Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Thai, Arabic, Greek, Hindi and Russian forms. All forms are equivalent, though using one “MAY be interpreted as an indication of the kind of coffee produced.”

The list in the memo is not perfect: it has a few typos and the text says “29 languages” while fewer are given. Section 2 also points to Section 4 for the URI scheme, which is actually Section 3.
sections.eli5: Just as web addresses start with http:, coffee machines get addresses that start with the word for coffee in whatever language you like.

sections.title: Operations and Management
sections.content:
The operational sections are mostly dry-humored commentary on real history. Coffee pots SHOULD use the Network Time Protocol to synchronize clocks, and the memo compares the protocol to remote monitoring of the Cambridge Trojan Room coffee pot, where a camera and frame-grabber put a coffee machine on the web.

It also covers caching: images of changing scenes need to be fetched fresh each time. Management is delegated to a Coffee Pot MIB, RFC 2325, published the same day.
sections.eli5: The document mentions a real coffee pot at a university that people watched over the internet to see if there was coffee left, and promises a separate rulebook for checking on coffee pots.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section opens with a joke: “Anyone who gets in between me and my morning coffee should be insecure.” It then lists threats in the same spirit: unprotected pots could face “denial of coffee service” attacks, improper filtration “might admit trojan grounds,” and grounds in Internet plumbing might require an Internet Plumber.

The substantive point hidden in the humor is that remotely controllable physical devices need access control. The memo ends with “Access authentication will be discussed in a separate memo.” No such memo followed.
sections.eli5: The jokes here are about bad guys stopping your coffee or clogging the pipes. The real idea is that if anyone online can start your machine, you should have a lock on it.

items.title: BREW
items.text: Starts or stops a pot via a message body. Servers must treat it the same as POST.

items.title: POST
items.text: Accepted equivalently, but deprecated for causing actions.

items.title: PROPFIND
items.text: Borrowed from WebDAV to discover metadata about the brewed resource.

items.title: WHEN
items.text: Said while milk is being poured, to mean “that’s enough.”

today: HTCPCP is not deployed as a real standard, but the joke lives on. The 418 I'm a teapot status is recognised by many web frameworks and tools, and is listed in the IANA HTTP status code registry. It was updated by RFC 7168, the April 2014 HTCPCP-TEA follow-up that adds tea support. The current HTTP specification, RFC 9110, treats 418 as a reserved code that implementations should not repurpose.
